title: MQM-P says will be approaching other parties to set off 'grand national dialogue' on new provinces
description: Party chairman says will engage lawyers to move the SC to take notice of the “desecration of its ruling” regarding local governments.
author: News Desk
content:
The Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) announced on Sunday that it was taking the initiative to approach other parties to begin a “grand national dialogue” on the creation of new provinces in the country.
MQM-P Chairman Dr Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui made the announcement at a press conference in Karachi, where he stressed the need for a grand national dialogue on the matter.
He said his party had been contending that the creation of existing provinces in Pakistan did not meet all legal merits and had a linguistic basis.
“We have been saying for the past 40 years […] that Pakistan’s existing provinces were not created in accordance with all merits of law and were made on linguistic grounds,” he said, adding that the country’s growing population also presented the need for the creation of new administrative units.
Siddiqui expressed gratitude that various political parties and groups were choosing to support MQM-P’s “long-standing” demand for more provinces.
He said that the objective of Sunday’s press conference was to give people the message that, “regardless of your political demands, start a dialogue with each other”.
“We will talk to various political parties — a grand national dialogue is needed regarding their suggestions and reservations on the matter,” he said. “We are initiating it,” he added.
Siddiqui said, “Wherever there is support for new provinces, we will stand with that voice.”
He went on to clarify that the MQM-P was not asking for new administrative units only in Sindh but across the country; however, he noted that the case for new provinces remained “strongest” in Sindh.
The MQM-P chairman also spoke of Article 140-A, which was added to the Constitution under the 18th Amendment in 2010. It requires provinces to devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility and authority to elected local representatives.
“We took part in the sin of the 18th Amendment [so] that a common Pakistani can reap the fruits of democracy through Article 140-A,” he said, lamenting the lack of its implementation.
He recalled that the party had moved the Supreme Court against the lack of implementation, “which issued a detailed ruling on the matter that was applicable across the country”.
Siddiqui held that the demand for stronger local governance was not limited to the MQM-P and stressed that it had rather become a “need” for Pakistan.
He said the MQM-P did not have “even a single councillor” in union councils across the country and reiterated that the implementation of Article 140-A was “not just a party demand” but rather a “constitutional requirement”.
Siddiqui recalled that when the MQM-P joined the coalition at the Centre, the party had one demand: “You must empower people to reap the fruits of democracy, meet constitutional requirements and implement the Supreme Court’s decision.”
Siddiqui questioned if the creation of additional provinces was such a “sin and an act of treason, then how is it mentioned in the Constitution?”
“Yes, we can discuss the method for creating provinces, but we believe that giving provinces that right is a conflict of interest,” he said. “Who would willingly allow the division of their property?” he asked rhetorically.
Concluding his address, the MQM-P chairman said the party will engage lawyers to move the SC to take notice of the “desecration of its ruling”.
Responding to a question over whether the creation of administrative units was equivalent to the division of Sindh, Siddiqui said, “When we came here, we brought our own Sindh with us, which is Matruka Sindh.”
“The Sindhi brothers who welcomed us […] we have immense respect for them in our hearts,” he said, claiming that 60 per cent of Sindh’s land was owned by Hindus, who had “migrated to India while we came here in their place. They took our properties there”.
At this, he reiterated, “We will remember your love, and if you want, we can even observe a thanksgiving day in the spirit of our respect for you”.
MQM-P leader and Health Minister Mustafa Kamal also spoke at the press conference and maintained that the call for administrative units was “not about division, but rather administrative rearrangement”.
He said his party was calling for a system where “people should have the right to vote for change in leadership if their city has been reduced to the third least livable city in the world”.
Kamal added that Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi’s proposal for more administrative units had been “music to our ears, as the people running the country are realising the creation of administrative units is the only way forward”.
Naqvi made the call last month while addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad.
The interior minister had urged all political parties to resolve various national issues, including the question of creating new provinces. He termed this the only solution to improving the country’s overall condition, which he said had “collapsed”.
A day later, the military’s spokesperson also called on political parties to consider an administrative reset to improve governance, arguing that the country’s security and stability depended on adapting its governance structure to the demands of modern times and a growing population.
Various political parties have also been demanding the creation of more provinces or administrative units for better governance.
The MQM-P has been demanding that Karachi be designated a province separate from Sindh. However, the PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre along with MQM-P, has strongly opposed the suggested move.
On the other hand, the PPP and the PTI have long advocated for a South Punjab province .
The issue gained momentum after Naqvi’s proposal drew strong reactions from government ministers, while the country’s leading lawyers’ bodies adopted divergent positions .
A top government functionary recently told Dawn that there is a serious debate underway in power corridors over the most feasible approach to creating new provinces. He believed the discussion is a precursor to the proposed 28th Constitutional Amendment .
The government source, who is privy to developments, was reluctant to say when the proposal — still said to be in the initial stages — could materialise.
He conceded, however, that turning the idea of new administrative into reality would not be easy, as building a consensus among major political parties, which appear opposed to the idea, would be a major challenge.
After MQM-P leaders’ Sunday press conference, PPP leader Qadir Mandokhail said his party was in favour of new provinces but warned against the division of Sindh, according to a statement issued via PPP’s X account.
“No political party can target the unity of Sindh for its own interests,” he was quoted as saying. Mandokhail warned that Sindh was not just a “line on a map” which could be divided on a whim.
Mandokhail said that it was a “sign of doomsday that people who had always played games of blood and fire in Sindh now appeared concerned for Sindh”.
“If they do not want to live with the people of Karachi, we can build them houses on the Sindh-Balochistan border.” Mandokhail recalled that the people of Sindh “had put to rest such slogans before”.
He held that the PPP will not allow anyone to “trample the constitution in the name of dividing Sindh”.
He slammed the MQM-P leadership for failing to have councillors in their respective constituencies. “Becoming a member of the National Assembly on a fake mandate does not make one an actual public representative,” he added.

title: Wells Fargo Reflect® Card Review
description: The Wells Fargo Reflect Card pairs a long 0% intro APR with no annual fee -- but no rewards. See who it&#39;s best for and top alternatives.
author: Joel O'Leary
content:

Joel O’Leary is a full-time Personal Finance Writer at Motley Fool Money, covering credit cards, bank accounts, investing, mortgages, and other personal finance topics. Joel has been writing about personal finance since 2018, previously leading editorial content for the How To Money podcast and serving as a resident writer at Budgets Are Sexy. He bought his first rental property at age 18, funding the down payment with savings from his high school job at McDonald’s -- a testament to his lifelong passion for smart money decisions. His work aims to make personal finance accessible and actionable for everyday readers. When he’s not writing, Joel enjoys surfing and spending time with his family.

The catch: once that intro APR window closes, the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card earns no rewards and hands you no ongoing perks. So it's not a great long-term keeper.
If your only goal is to stop interest cold, the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card is hard to beat. Here's my honest review.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card is best for people carrying high-interest debt or planning a large purchase they want to spread out over time.
You get nearly two years of breathing room with no interest, which can save a lot of money while you pay things off.
If you're looking for cash back or travel rewards, this is not the card for you. The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card has no rewards program and no welcome bonus. It loses most of its value the moment the intro period ends.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card's headline feature is 0% intro APR for 21 months from account opening on purchases and qualifying balance transfers. (A 17.49%, 23.99%, or 28.24% Variable APR applies after.)
That's one of the longest 0% APR periods you'll find anywhere -- which is why it earned Motley Fool Money's award for Best 0% Intro APR Card of 2026.
This long intro APR is particularly handy for large balances (think anything $5,000+). The longer the promo window, the less you need to pay each month to clear your balance while paying no interest.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges no annual fee, so it costs nothing to keep in your wallet. For anyone building credit history -- or, like me, holding onto a top credit card for the long haul -- that's a real plus.
Keeping the card open can help your credit score by lengthening your average credit history over time.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card includes cellphone protection when you pay your monthly phone bill with the card. It covers up to $600 per claim for theft or damage, with a $25 deductible, and you can file up to two claims per 12-month period.
I've never had to use cellphone insurance, but as a frequent phone-dropper and generally clumsy person, I've always loved having it in my back pocket.

The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card earns no rewards. If you want a card with long-term perks like cash back or travel points, this isn't it.
A strong alternative is the Wells Fargo Active Cash® Card ( rates and fees ), which earns a flat 2% cash rewards on purchases for a $0 annual fee. It's our Best Overall Credit Card of 2026, and a fan favorite for flat-rate rewards .
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges a balance transfer fee of 5%, min: $5 -- this is on the high side for a balance transfer card.
If you move a $10,000 balance, you'd owe a $500 fee, even though you'd pay the balance off at 0% during the intro period.
Run the math before you transfer, because the fee should cost less than the interest you'd otherwise pay. If you won't clear the balance within the 0% APR period, then an alternative balance transfer card with a lower transfer fee may serve you better.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card charges a 3% foreign transaction fee, so you'll pay extra on purchases made outside the U.S. If you travel abroad and want to skip that cost, consider one of our favorite travel credit cards .
It also has no purchase protection or extended warranty on purchases.
You'll generally need good to excellent credit (Motley Fool Money estimates this to be a FICO® Score of about 670 or higher) to qualify for the Wells Fargo Reflect® Card. Wells Fargo doesn't publish an official cutoff, and applicants closer to 700 tend to be the best-qualified candidates.
Keep in mind, your score isn't the only factor. Wells Fargo also weighs your income, existing debt, and overall credit history. You can check for pre-selected offers on Wells Fargo's site without a hard inquiry to gauge your chances first.
The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card comes with a minimum credit limit of $1,000, and higher scores and income generally earn higher limits. Wells Fargo sets your limit individually based on your full credit profile, so two applicants can get very different lines of credit.
Your starting limit isn't permanent, though. Once your account is open and in good standing, usually after six to 12 months, you can request an increase. Or, Wells Fargo may raise it automatically for on-time payments and low utilization.
To get the 0% intro APR for 21 months from account opening on qualifying balance transfers (then 17.49%, 23.99%, or 28.24% Variable APR), you must complete qualifying transfers within 120 days of opening your account.
I recommend starting the transfer online or by phone as soon as you're approved. Having your old account details ready speeds things up.
One important note: you can't transfer a balance from another Wells Fargo or affiliated card. Transfers have to come from a different issuer, and the 5%, min: $5 transfer fee applies to each one.

When the 0% intro APR period ends, any remaining balance starts accruing interest at your regular variable APR from that point forward. The Wells Fargo Reflect® Card doesn't charge deferred or retroactive interest, so you only pay on what's left -- not on the full original balance.

Keeping the card open is usually the better move, even after your balance hits $0. If it has no annual fee, it costs nothing to hold, and the open account helps your credit score by supporting your total available credit and length of history.

title: Reform proposes Â£50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments system Pip
description: The party's proposed changes were they to come to power include a replacement for the disability payments system Pip.
author: Harry Farley, Imogen James
content:
Jenrick said Reform will not pretend the plans are painless
Reform UK says it would aim to cut about Â£50bn from the benefits bill and replace the disability payments system, Pip, if it comes in to government.
Robert Jenrick, the party's treasury spokesperson, said the plans, to be set out in full on Monday, would be the most comprehensive overhaul to the welfare system in a generation and affect nearly three million people.
In an article for the Sunday Telegraph , external he said the current system is "suicidal empathy" and "a strange perversion of compassion".
Labour said it was "fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people", while the Conservatives called it a "half-baked policy" and another "attempt to distract from" questions about the Â£5m gift party leader Nigel Farage received.
Reform's plans include making companies pay for any employees off sick for the first two years. Businesses with more than five employees would have to take out insurance to cover the cost.
Reform says this is modelled on the Dutch system and would incentivise employers to make adaptions and encourage people back to work to reduce their insurance premiums.
The party says they would cut the National Insurance contributions (NICs) paid by employers to offset the cost of this measure, insisting the change would be cost neutral for businesses.
In a policy document to be published next week, which the BBC has seen an extract of, the party estimates 2.89 million people would have their disability payments' removed, or modified, under plans to abolish Personal Independent Payments (Pip) for working age people.
The party would also remove the extra health-related payments on Universal Credit.
A new system, called a Health Security Allowance, would replace both Pip and the Universal Credit health element but only the most "severe, enduring and high-risk cases" would receive cash support, the document says.
Other claimants would be supported through a council-run programme to cover what Reform said would be the "verifiable additional costs" as a result of their disability.
To boost available support for people out of work, the party says it would spend an extra Â£1.85bn a year on interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy, physiotherapy, and employment support.
Reform also wants to reform children's benefits, and is promising to align the system for anxiety, depression and ADHD in young people with its changes to the adult system. But this would only apply to new claimants.
Welfare cuts: What's been happening with Pip and universal credit?
Reform UK pledges to cut welfare to keep pensions triple lock
In March 2025, the government attempted to tighten the daily living assessments for both current and future claimants, but was forced to dial back after pressure from Labour MPs.
Jenrick described this as an attempt at "modest savings" gutted by backbenchers.
Last month, an interim report was published by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms, who has been leading a review into Pip, stating the benefit was "not fit for purpose" and requires a fundamental change .
A Labour spokesperson said: "Reform's Â£50bn claim is fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people and shifting costs onto employers.
"Labour is already reforming welfare: narrowing the gap between Universal Credit standard and health rates, restoring face-to-face assessments, and investing Â£3.5bn in employment support to end the culture of people being signed off and written off."
The Conservative's shadow welfare secretary Helen Whately said: "This half-baked policy is just another Reform attempt to distract from Farage's fishy Â£5m and his embarrassing underperformance in his pointless by-election."
A parliamentary standards investigation is taking place into a Â£5m gift given to the Reform leader from a donor before he became an MP, with Farage saying the money did not need to be registered. The investigation was paused after Farage resigned as Clacton MP in response to the scrutiny of his financial backing, triggering a by-election last week, which he won.

title: Fire services 'under pressure' as evacuated residents still not home
description: Major incidents declared across England and Wales with blazes in Stourbridge, Sandwell and Pershore.
author: Susie Rack, Joan Cummins, Christopher Steers
content:
A total of 38 homes have been destroyed or damaged in Stourbridge
Eleven major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure", a fire boss has said.
Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said major incidents had been declared across the UK, including in Stourbridge, Sandwell, Pershore and Stoke-on-Trent in the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and South Wales.
In Stourbridge, 38 houses have been destroyed or damaged by the fires, with some residents left unable to return home.
West Midlands Fire Service set up a meeting point on Saturday where residents would be told if their house had been damaged or totally destroyed in the blaze and if it was safe to go back.
Public urged to avoid 'surrounded' New Forest fire site
What we know so far about the West Midlands fires
West Midlands Assistant Chief Fire Officer Simon Barry told residents the fire there was under control and they were just dampening down hot spots.
He said as far as the service was concerned, homes were no longer at risk and he hoped some residents whose homes had been unaffected would be able to move back on Saturday evening.
In a recorded online briefing, Dudley Council chief executive Balvinder Hera stressed residents should not return home until explicitly told they could do so.
She said decisions to reopen roads were being taken on a street-by-street basis, with the council working closely with emergency services.
Police were keen to hear from people with information or video footage that could assist inquiries and had asked the public not to speculate on the fire's cause, she said.
An online fund , external has been set up by the council to allow people to donate to those affected.
Three hundred residents were evacuated in Stourbridge, with many still not home
West Midlands Fire and Rescue Service was alerted to the large grass fire near Stourbridge Golf Club in the Racecourse Lane area just before 13:30 BST on Thursday.
More than 100 firefighters fought the flames across an area of 500 acres, with hotspots remaining on Saturday.
John Moore was asked to leave his home on Osmaston Road as fire spread through grass and woodland about half a mile away.
He said he was now visiting the cordon four times a day to seek information.
"It's absolutely shocking. We can get no answers about when we can go back," he said.
The house he shares with his 86-year-old wife, who is partially bedridden, was not damaged, but he has only been permitted to visit it to pick up medication.
Moore said: "There's probably about 60 other people who are normally here by the side of me every day asking, 'can we go?'."
John Moore has visited the cordon multiple times each day to seek answers
Simon Tuhill from West Midlands Fire Service said 19 properties had been "completely destroyed", with a further 19 damaged.
He said specialist investigators were on the scene and working with police to try to "triangulate down where the fire started".
Other residents who have lost everything gathered at a cordon at the corner of Worcester Road and Racecourse Lane, frustrated by the lack of information and not being allowed to see what had become of their homes.
One man told the BBC he had met Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday when he visited the region, saying Burnham had promised to personally intervene to help his family get their passports.
A woman described suffering horrific flashbacks and claimed it had taken 40 minutes for a fire engine to respond to her emergency call.
Meanwhile, A-level student Dominic Abdullah was forced to flee shortly after he had got his results on Thursday.
"I thought the day couldn't get any more big, any more significant," he said.
This video can not be played
Student evacuates home after receiving A-level results
A national government alert sent out by the government on Friday warned people not to light anything that might spark a fire.
Garrigan said the NFCC had asked politicians to highlight the risks fire services were facing, with control room operators dealing with "thousands and thousands of calls".
He said services had been unable to immediately meet demand at points during the busiest 24-hour period from Thursday afternoon.
"They'd asked for maybe 10 additional appliances to come in nationally, and we weren't able to provide them with the full 10 in the first instance," he said.
He added firefighters were "still seeing fires occur through maybe carelessness or deliberate action".
Marie Leese's treasured garden was destroyed by flames
Elsewhere in the West Midlands, in Goldenhill, Stoke-on-Trent, four homes in Sandyford were destroyed on Thursday, with other nearby properties damaged.
Marie Leese escaped the fire with just her dog and her phone, but her beloved garden on Maureen Avenue was destroyed, including a summer house built by her husband before he died.
"It was like the scenes of the Blitz, just a blazing inferno, the flames were moving so quickly," she said.
"I feel fortunate that I've been allowed back, but the house across the road still has hotspots and is destroyed."
She said she was too terrified to sleep, because the neighbouring house "keeps reigniting".
Two people have been arrested by Staffordshire Police on suspicion of arson in connection with the incident.
In Clun, Shropshire, firefighters spent the night tackling a fire on Black Hill.
An emergency presence was expected in the area for some time as hot spots were put out.
"As you can imagine, the thick forestry makes this type of fire incredibly challenging to tackle," said Clun Fire Station on social media.
And in the Peak District a fire in Totley Rail Tunnel between Totley, Sheffield, and Grindleford, has led to all lines being closed.

title: MQM-P urges national dialogue to finalise framework for creation of new provinces
description: MQM-P says population growth demands new administrative units.Party may approach Supreme Court over stalled provinces issue.PM's adviser rejects consideration of any plan for new provinces.Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan Chairman...
author: Web Desk
content:
Published August 16, 2026
Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) Chairman Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui on Sunday called for a national dialogue on the creation of new provinces, saying Pakistan's existing administrative structure no longer corresponds to the country's demographic realities and governance requirements.
The call comes amid a renewed debate on administrative reforms after Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi proposed last month the creation of new administrative units, arguing that Pakistan's "collapsed" governance structure requires restructuring to meet growing administrative challenges.
Siddiqui, addressing a press conference alongside senior MQM-P leaders Dr Farooq Sattar and Mustafa Kamal in Karachi, urged political parties to rise above partisan differences and build a consensus on administrative reforms.
He argued that the issue should be addressed through an inclusive national discussion rather than political confrontation.
He said support for the proposal was growing across the political spectrum, adding that MQM-P was prepared to engage with all stakeholders to develop a framework for the establishment of new provinces where they were needed.
Siddiqui maintained that Pakistan's provinces were originally formed on linguistic considerations and had since evolved into large administrative units.
Despite substantial population growth over the decades, he said, successive governments had created numerous districts while avoiding a broader debate on provincial reorganisation.
"The effects of not creating new provinces should also be discussed," he said, arguing that administrative boundaries should reflect population size and governance needs.
He added that Sindh was among the regions where the demand for additional administrative units was most pronounced.
The MQM-P chairman rejected the notion that advocating new provinces was controversial, noting that the Constitution itself contains provisions relating to the creation of provinces. "If it is considered an act of disloyalty, then why does the Constitution provide for it?" he asked.
Referring to the 18th Constitutional Amendment, Siddiqui said his party supported the reforms to ensure that the benefits of democracy reached all parts of the country.
He argued, however, that the objectives of decentralisation could not be fully realised without strengthening administrative structures at the provincial level.
He said MQM-P had already introduced a constitutional bill on the issue, which remains before a parliamentary standing committee, and recalled that the party had previously sought judicial intervention when progress stalled.
Siddiqui said MQM-P would continue supporting calls for new provinces from different parts of the country and remained open to dialogue with all political parties.
He also indicated that the party could again approach the Supreme Court if constitutional and legal obligations regarding the matter remained unfulfilled.
Kamal said that the creation of additional administrative units was not aimed against any ethnic group, including Sindhis, but was intended to improve governance and public representation.
He said a more decentralised administrative structure would give citizens greater influence over local governance and strengthen accountability.
Addressing the presser, Sattar said the establishment of additional administrative units has become essential for the country's stability and cohesion.
He was of the view that bringing governance closer to citizens would improve public participation, enhance service delivery and ensure that local leadership emerged from the areas it represented.
The proposal has, however, elicited mixed reactions across the political spectrum. The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), which governs Sindh and is a key coalition partner of the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), has firmly opposed the creation of new provinces.
Senior government figures, including Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and Prime Minister's Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah, have also refrained from endorsing the idea.
As the debate gathered momentum, Naqvi moved to clarify his earlier remarks, rejecting suggestions that he had criticised the government. He said he was part of the administration and would not issue a "charge sheet" against his own government.
Speaking to Geo News , the interior minister had said the current system would continue and complete its constitutional term, stressing that his comments about a "collapsed" governance structure referred to the gradual erosion of administrative and institutional capacity over the past eight decades rather than the performance of the present government.
A day ago, Sanaullah said that the government had not formulated any plan regarding the creation of new provinces.
Speaking on Geo News programme Naya Pakistan, he noted that various proposals were being floated publicly, with some advocating 12 provinces, others 20, and some even more.
He said MQM-P leader and Federal Minister Kamal's proposal was primarily focused on Karachi, adding that the PML-N's top leadership had not discussed the issue in recent days.
He also questioned the level of public support for the proposal, arguing that there was no widespread demand for new provinces across the country. Apart from calls for a Hazara province, he said, there was little evidence of a broader grassroots movement in favour of provincial reorganisation.
The proposal has, however, found support in some political quarters. Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP) President Abdul Aleem Khan backed the creation of new provinces, describing it as a national issue that should not be sacrificed for political expediency.
He also voiced support for the establishment of South Punjab and Bahawalpur provinces, saying demands for additional administrative units were emerging from different parts of the country.
Major opposition party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan also endorsed the idea, saying the country required additional administrative units.
He stressed, however, that any move to create new provinces should be based on broad political consensus and carried out through the constitutional process, including approval by the requisite two-thirds majority in the relevant assemblies.

title: Security forces kill 7 terrorists in IBO in Balochistan's Kharan: state media
description: Security sources say weapons, ammunition, two vehicles and a motorcycle recovered from terrorists’ hideouts.
author: News Desk
content:
Security forces killed seven terrorists in an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in Balochistan’s Kharan, state media reported on Sunday, citing security sources.
The IBO was carried out in the district’s Lajay area under Operation Radd-ul-Fitna 3, during which several terrorists were also injured, state-run Pakistan TV reported.
It added that security sources said weapons, ammunition, two vehicles and a motorcycle were recovered from the terrorists’ hideouts.
President Asif Ali Zardari, in a statement on social media, paid tribute to the successful operation by the security forces, calling the destruction of terrorist hideouts and recovery of arms and ammunition an “important achievement”.
“Actions against terrorist elements active under foreign patronage are indispensable for safeguarding national security,” the president said.
“The entire nation stands with Pakistan’s security forces in this war against terrorism,” he added.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi praised the security forces for the success of the operation and appreciated their professional capabilities, his ministry said in a statement posted to X.
“The remarkable successes achieved by the security forces in establishing peace in Balochistan are commendable,” the ministry’s statement said, adding that the IBOs would continue “until the last terrorist is eliminated”.
On Saturday, security forces also killed 10 terrorists and injured many others in an IBO in the Shor Pard area of Balochistan’s Khuzdar district.
Likewise, at least 18 terrorists were killed in Balochistan’s Surab district, including eight in a premature detonation, the miliatry’s media affairs wing said on Wednesday, and state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported earlier this week that five terrorists, including a key commander, were killed in an IBO in the Sarkini and Chedgi areas of Panjgur district.
The operations are the latest in a string of actions being taken as Balochistan continues to grapple with security challenges.
According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment released on July 31, the security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan in the country last month.
The overall death toll increased by 241pc in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the report said.
Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province.

title: Naqvi comes to CDA chairman, Islamabad IG's defence as they draw flak over buggy video with 'colonial' undertone
description: Naqvi says that the carriage was arranged for the chief guest but had to be used by officers "due to unavoidable circumstances".
author: News Desk
content:
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday came to the defence of two government officials who drew flak after a video of them riding in a horse carriage during an Independence Day parade in Islamabad went viral on social media.
In the widely circulated video, Capital Development Authority (CDA) Chairman retired Lt Sohail Ashraf and the Islamabad Inspector General of Police (IGP) Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi are seen riding into the parade in what appears to be the presidential buggy. Even as the attendees are prompted to applaud for the officials, no claps are heard in the video.
The video sparked criticism on social media, with many likening the act to a “colonial” mindset.
Meanwhile, Naqvi issued a clarification on X, stating that it was not the officials’ fault.
“The chief guest and I were delayed due to the president’s meeting with the prime minister. The crowd had been waiting since 5pm, and at around 6:00 pm, when it became clear that we would be late, we instructed the officers to start the programme because we did not want the public to wait any longer.”
Naqvi maintained that the carriage was arranged for the chief guest but had to be used by officers “due to unavoidable circumstances”.
“I can say on record that both officers initially resisted starting the programme in our absence, but we specifically instructed them to proceed for the convenience of the public,” he said, adding that he remained grateful to the residents of Islamabad for making the event “a true celebration”.
But others continued with the criticism. Even after his clarification, former federal minister Shireen Mazari shared a post by digital rights activist Usama Khilji that included the video and said, “Unbelievably stupid to try and revive such colonial practices! Self-humiliation!”
Khilji, in his post, criticised the two officials, saying, “This is what happens when you do things unbecoming of your office”.
He added, “Pakistan’s political class has its problems, but at the end of the day they have to pander to citizens for support, votes and legitimacy; however flawed. Civil and military bureaucracy, on the other hand, functions with complete impunity, much like the British Raj from which we inherited them.”
Journalist Farzana Ali, reacting to the video, questioned: “Are these scenes from the same country where a new burden is imposed on poverty-stricken people every day on the pretext that the country is facing difficulties?”
Journalist Zarrar Khuhro also shared the video with a one-word caption: “CRINGE”.
Researcher Ammar Rashid stressed that the “pindrop silence” from the audience at the carriage’s arrival indicated the “contempt” the public had for “these unelected babus ruining our cities”.
“Anti-people DC Raj needs to go,” he wrote on X .
Journalist and former chairman of the Pakistan Electronic Media Authority (Pemra) Absar Alam also reacted to the video, saying it was “revolting” to look at the “inferiority complex of brown sahibs of bureaucracy”.
Former Sindh governor and Awaam Pakistan leader Mohammad Zubair juxtaposed the video against one showing the Norwegian foreign minister’s arrival in Islamabad earlier this week. The minister was said to have handled his luggage on his own at the airport.
“What a contrast — difference in the behaviour between the top minister of the richest country versus grade 22 officials of one of the poorest countries,” commented Zubair on X.
Political analyst Zaigham Khan shared a similar video, saying: “Once upon a time, this was a symbol of immense grandeur and splendour. Today, it brings nothing but humiliation, yet even this much about our changing society hasn’t dawned on our owners.”
Journalist Fahd Husain, reacting to the video, said, “This clip reminds us system won’t be reformed till bureaucracy is reformed”.
“The current bureaucratic structure is a relic of the past and must be thoroughly changed,” he wrote.

title: Indonesia: Thousands displaced by deadly earthquake as rescue efforts continue
description: Hundreds of homes and public buildings have been severely damaged with at least 53 people killed.
author: Emma Rossiter
content:
This video can not be played
Watch: Buildings partially collapse in Indonesia after 7.7 earthquake
Around 5,000 people have been displaced by a powerful earthquake in Indonesia that has caused at least 53 fatalities.
Rescuers continue to search for survivors of the shallow magnitude 7.7 quake, which struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 local time on Saturday (22:00 GMT on Friday).
Preliminary reports indicate more than 900 homes and hundreds of other buildings have been severely damaged by the tremor and 341 subsequent aftershocks, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) said.
The full scale of the disaster is still being uncovered, with news of a second magnitude 6.9 earthquake elsewhere in Indonesia serving as a reminder of why this region is called the ring of fire.
The initial earthquake, which occurred just 15km below the surface, was the south-east Asian nation's deadliest since 2022, when hundreds of people were killed in West Java.
Tremors were reportedly felt by residents as far west as Bima, the BNPB said, but the Manggarai province was among the most affected.
Abdul Muhari, deputy for the BNPB, confirmed 25 deaths had been recorded there, as well as 20 fatalities in East Manggarai province, four in Sikka province, two in Ende and at least one person in both the Nagekeo and West Manggarai provinces.
A total of 3,356 people had been displaced in Sikka, with a further 2,078 evacuated in Manggarai, the agency said.
Thirty-six people were seriously injured in East Nusa Tenggara province, while 77 suffered minor injuries, Deputy Health Minister Benjamin Paulus Octavianus said.
It will take time to assess the full extent of the destruction in the region, which is remote and mountainous.
The area is mountainous and the assessment will take time, officials say
However, early reports indicate that, in addition to damaged homes, dozens of schools, healthcare facilities and government offices had also been severely damaged.
Ruteng Regional Hospital in Manggarai was among them. Images show operating theatre and clinic ceilings caved in, requiring patients to be treated in tents.
"We heard that medical assistance would be provided, but nothing has arrived yet," hospital spokesperson Rista Mari told BBC Indonesian. "We hope that assistance will arrive soon."
The BNPB said "meeting basic needs and providing logistics for evacuees has become one of the top priorities of the emergency response", adding it had dispatched tonnes of emergency supplies to Manggarai.
Video taken at the port in Maumere - the largest town in Flores - showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed.
Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that several of the victims had been killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble.
Others, like Arnold Welianto, who lives in Talibura, a village near the coastline in Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara, were shaken out of their beds.
"I was startled awake and immediately went to my child's room," he said.
He also told the BBC that many people had already fled into the hills because the sea had also receded.
The earthquake struck around 600 miles (1,000km) away from Bali
Rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble
While a tsunami warning was initially issued - leading some 2,000 people to self-evacuate - it was lifted around three hours after the initial jolt, when no significant sea level rise was detected.
Landslides, however, did block access to some villages but the experienced rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble.
In Ruteng, a temporary medical tent was also assembled outside of a hospital to treat earthquake victims.
People could be seen moving inland after authorities issued a tsunami warning, which was later lifted
The ongoing advice from BNPB is for people to remain calm and to stay away from coastal areas and structures showing signs of damage.
Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates.

title: April 3, 2023 - Russia-Ukraine news
description: A female suspect has been detained in connection with an explosion that killed a prominent Russian military blogger at a cafe in St. Petersburg on Sunday.
author: Tara Subramaniam, Jack Guy, Aditi Sangal, Maureen Chowdhury, Mike Hayes
content:
Our live coverage for the day has ended. Follow the latest Ukraine news here or read through the updates below.
The preventive detention hearing for Daria Trepova , who was detained in connection with the explosion at a cafe in St. Petersburg, Russia, will take place on Tuesday at Basmanny District Court in Moscow, according to Russian state news agency Vesti.
Russian authorities detained Trepova, 26, claiming she was involved in the blast that killed well-known military blogger Vladlen Tatarsky at a café in St. Petersburg on Sunday.
The US Ambassador to the United Nations Linda Thomas-Greenfield on Monday described Russia assuming the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) presidency this month as “an April Fool’s joke.”
Greenfield said she is not surprised if the Russians asked the foreign minister to come to UNSC headquarters in New York but also said council does work beyond Ukraine.
“We haven’t decided yet on what our attendance levels will be, but we intend to carry out the business of the Security Council during this month. The Security Council does more than Ukraine. We work on many issues, and we again expect that Russia will carry their presidency in a professional way, but when they don’t, we will stand ready to call them out,” Greenfield said.
Vasily Nebenzya , Russian ambassador to the United Nations, dismissed concerns that Russia could fairly be the president of the Security Council for April during the ongoing war in Ukraine.
He said there were no complaints in February 2022 when Russia was last president of the council, while Russia invaded and pointed out that the US was president of the council in 2003 — the year Iraq was invaded.
The ambassador said as long as world order is maintained, there will not be any change in UN procedures that might lead to a change in Russia’s status.
Russia took over presidency on Saturday of the UN’s top security body, which rotates every month.
Here are the latest headlines:
Newly published video shows the moments running up to an explosion that killed Russian military journalist Vladen Tartovsky in a St Petersburg café on Sunday.
Tatarsky died when a blast tore through the cafe where he was appearing as a guest of a pro-war group called Cyber Front Z. Prior Russian media reports suggested that Tatarsky may have been killed by a device hidden in a figurine presented to him by a woman before the blast.
The 25-second video shows Tartovsky putting a statuette given to him at the event into a box after passing the microphone to another man.
He places the statuette back into the box and then covers it with what appears to be paper wrapping. As he presses down the paper, there is an explosion.
In the last two seconds of the video, Tartovsky is pixillated, but the rest of the scene is not.
More to know: The well-known Russian blogger was killed in what appeared to be an audacious attack on a high-profile pro-Kremlin figure, officials said.
Authorities said they were treating the case as suspected murder.
At least 32 people were injured in the blast, with 10 people in serious condition, state media Ria Novosti reported, citing the Russian Ministry of Health.
Russian ambassador to the United Nations Vasily Nebenzya on Monday scoffed at concerns that his country could fairly be the president of the Security Council for April during the war in Ukraine.
Nebenzya pointed out that the US was president of the council in 2003 — the year Iraq was invaded.
He said there were no complaints in February 2022 when Russia was last president of the council, while Russia invaded.
Ukraine has received the first tranche of $2.7 billion from a new International Monetary Fund (IMF) program, Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said in a tweet Monday.
The IMF, which regularly makes emergency loans to countries in crisis, on Friday approved a new four-year extended arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) of around $15.6 billion as part of a $115 billion total support package for Ukraine.
The program aims to “anchor policies that sustain fiscal, external, price and financial stability and support economic recovery, while enhancing governance and strengthening institutions to promote long-term growth in the context of post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s path to EU accession,” the IMF said in a statement .
The program also helps Ukraine to carry out “more ambitious structural reforms,” it said.
The Extended Fund Facility (EFF) loan is the first major conventional financing program approved by the IMF for a country involved in a large-scale war, Reuters reported.
The risks to the arrangement are “exceptionally high,” said Gita Gopinath, first deputy managing director of the global lender.
“The success of the program depends on the size, composition, and timing of external financing on concessional terms to help close fiscal and external financing gaps and restore debt sustainability on a forward-looking basis under the baseline and downside scenarios,” she added.
German Chancellor Olaf Scholz on Monday assured Moldova of Berlin’s support on its path to accession to the European Union as Moldovan and American officials allege Russia of trying to weaken the government in Chisinau.
“Moldova can be sure of our support on this path. I assured the President [Sandu] of this once again today. Moldova does not stand alone, but receives massive international support,” the German chancellor continued.
Scholz expressed “great concern” about reports of alleged Russian attempts to destabilize Moldova and said Germany would do its “utmost” to support Moldova in arming itself against “attempts of destabilization by Russia.”
In February, Moldova’s President Sandu accused Russia of planning to use “saboteurs who have undergone military training and are disguised as civilians” to destabilize the country — claims which were rejected by Russia’s foreign ministry as “unfounded.”
According to White House officials, the US believes that Russia is working to weaken the Moldovan government, as it continues to seek closer ties with the European Union.
“The sovereignty and territorial integrity of any state is inviolable. This requirement of the Helsinki Final Act and other agreements under international law was also signed by Russia. And it is still valid. Therefore, we do our utmost to support Moldova in arming itself against attempts of destabilization by Russia,” Scholz said.
Speaking at the same event, Sandu said that “it is very important, and I am happy that Moldova is a dialogue partner with Romania and Germany. The projects we are involved in together are very useful for our people and will strongly lead us to the accession (to the European Union).”
CNN’s Radina Gigova, Anna Chernova and Natasha Bertrand contributed reporting to this post.
NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said Monday that the alliance has not seen any changes in Russia’s nuclear posture since Russian President Vladimir Putin announced late last month Moscow’s plans to station tactical nuclear weapons in neighboring Belarus.
Stoltenberg described Putin’s announcement as a “pattern of dangerous, reckless nuclear rhetoric.”
“President Putin tries to use nuclear weapons as a way to prevent us from supporting Ukraine… intimidation, coercion to stop NATO Allies and partners for supporting Ukraine in their right to defend their own country,” he said.
NATO’s chief Jens Stoltenberg said on Monday that Western allies have delivered more than $70 billion in military aid to Ukraine over the last year since the Russian invasion started.
“We do not know when this war will end. But when it does, we will need to put in place arrangements so that Ukraine can deter future aggression. And history does not repeat itself. We cannot allow Russia to continue to chip away at European security,” he said.
Stoltenberg added that allies have delivered 65 billion euros (around $70.7 billion) in military aid, and said he welcomed the recent arrival of modern battle tanks and other armored vehicles in Ukraine.
“This can make a real difference on the front lines and allow the Ukrainian forces to liberate more territory,” he said.
The NATO head affirmed that the alliance’s support is for the “long haul” and said, “we will discuss how we can step up our support, including by continuing to strengthen Ukraine’s armed forces and supporting the transition from Soviet-era to NATO equipment and doctrine.”
Stoltenberg also said allies must address other threats and challenges, citing instability, terrorism, and the growing influence of Iran, Russia, and China. He urged allies to invest more in defense to tackle all these wide range of issues.
Norway and Denmark will cooperate to donate 8,000 artillery rounds to Ukraine, the Norwegian government announced in a statement on Monday.
“Norway donates the shells, while Denmark donates the associated fuzes, propellant bags and primer cartridges,” the statement said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reacted to the announcement, saying in a tweet that he was grateful for the donation.
The rounds will be “standard NATO 155 mm artillery ammunition and will supplement the Danish donation of 19 Caesar self-propelled howitzers,” Norway’s statement added.
Norway’s artillery shells will be delivered from the country’s armed forces’ own stock, according to the statement.
Norwegian defense minister Bjørn Arild Gram said “Ukraine has a significant need for artillery ammunition. Norway will contribute where we can. It is important for both Europe’s and Norway’s security that Ukraine succeeds in standing up to Russia’s attack.”
“The Ukrainians still have a great and urgent need for ammunition for their fight for freedom against Russia. Denmark, together with other EU and NATO countries, is in the process of accommodating with a number of different military contributions. Our cooperation with Norway is an important example of this,” the Danish acting defense minister, Troels Lund Poulsen, said in the statement.
The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.
The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.
It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.
“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.
West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.
Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”
Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”
Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.
“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.
He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.
“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.
He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”
Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.
Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.
“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
The war in Ukraine has cost an estimated $2.6 billion of damage to heritage and cultural sites in the country, the UN cultural body UNESCO said in a recently published report .
The report, which covers one year of war in Ukraine between February 24, 2022, and February 24, 2023, was a joint assessment conducted by the Ukrainian government, the World Bank, the European Commission, and the United Nations.
UNESCO was in charge of the part of the report dedicated to culture and tourism.
Some $1.7 billion of that cost was distributed to “historic cities, buildings, and sites imbued with recognized cultural/social values,” $650 million to tourism facilities, $143 million to “movable cultural properties and collections, repositories of culture,” and $150 million to “buildings/workshops/ateliers dedicated to cultural and creative industries,” according to UNESCO.
The most impacted region in Ukraine was Kharkivska, which has suffered 30% of the total damage to its cultural assets, the report added.
UNESCO said that losses are estimated at around $15.2 billion, which includes revenue losses from tourism, art, sports, entertainment, recreation, cultural education, and creative and cultural industries.
UNESCO’s head Audrey Azoulay is currently in Ukraine, the organization told CNN on Monday.
NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg said it will be historic when the military alliance raises the Finnish flag for the first time at its headquarters on Tuesday.
“It will be a good day for Finland’s security, for Nordic security, and for NATO as a whole,” Stoltenberg added.
Finland is set to become a member of the alliance on Tuesday, with Finnish President Sauli Niinistö traveling to Brussels to attend an accession ceremony at NATO headquarters.
Stoltenberg also spoke about Sweden’s bid to join NATO, saying Finland’s accession is “in itself something we should celebrate” but is also good for Sweden.
“It makes Sweden more integrated into NATO and makes Sweden even more safer,” Stoltenberg said, adding “at the same time we celebrate and enjoy that Finland is now full-fledged member, we should continue work to finalize the Swedish accession process.”
CNN’s Laurent Kent contributed to this report.
At least 501 children have been killed in Ukraine since February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion, said Catherine Russell, executive director of the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF).
“Another tragic milestone for Ukraine’s children and families,” Russell said in a tweet on Monday.
Russell warned the real figure is “likely far higher” than the numbers verified by the UN agency.
Additionally, almost 1,000 Ukrainian children have been injured, “leaving them with wounds and scars - both visible and invisible - that could last for life,” she added.
The head of the United Nations nuclear agency, International Atomic Energy Agency, will travel to the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad in the Baltics Wednesday to discuss the safety of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, a spokesperson for the agency told CNN.
“IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi will visit Kaliningrad on Wednesday as part of his ongoing consultations aimed at ensuring the protection of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant during the military conflict,” the spokesperson said Monday.
The plant has been occupied by Russian forces since March of last year and is now run by the Russian atomic agency, Rosatom.
The situation at the nuclear plant has not improved, according to the IAEA chief, who visited the facility last week and cited increased military activity in the area.
Grossi during the visit said he was trying to formulate “realistic, viable proposals” that would be acceptable to both sides.
Twelve Ukrainian prisoners have been returned home from captivity – 10 military and two civilians, Ukraine says.
Five of them were seriously wounded, according to the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War.
The soldiers were captured in various parts of the front lines, it added.
The Russian decision showed “a blatant lack of interest in establishing further exchanges for particularly vulnerable categories of prisoners and civilian hostages,” the headquarters said.
Since the beginning of the invasion in February last year, 2,005 Ukrainians have been released from captivity, according to the headquarters.
Wagner boss Yevgeny Prigozhin said Monday that he “gave” the St. Petersburg cafe, where an explosion killed Russian military blogger Vladlen Tatarsky on Sunday, to the Cyber Front Z group, which hosted an event at the cafe.
When asked to confirm whether he was the owner of the cafe, Prigozhin didn’t deny it, in comments published Monday by his holding company Concord on its VK social media page.
“Indeed, I gave the cafe to the patriotic movement Cyber Front Z, and they held various seminars there,” Prigozhin said.
Russia’s independent news outlet Fontanka is reporting that the cafe belongs to Prigozhin, on the basis of the Concord company’s ownership mentioned on the cafe’s receipt.
Prigozhin is the founder and sole owner of Concord, according to public records.
CNN has not been able to independently verify Prigozhin’s claims and whether he is the legal owner of the cafe.
In the same post, Prigozhin is also commenting on who may be behind the blast.
“I do not know the details of the incident now, I was only informed that, unfortunately, Vladlen Tatarsky died. I don’t know about the rest of the details,” Prigozhin said.
“Most likely, this tragedy happened at the seminar. As for the death of Darya Dugina, yes, everything is similar,” he said referencing the death of the daughter of ultra-nationalist philosopher Alexander Dugin, who was killed by a car bomb on the outskirts of Moscow last year.
“But I would not blame the Kyiv regime for these actions. I think that there is a group of radicals that is hardly related to the government. That’s what I would call it,” Prigozhin said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has declined to make any comment about the explosion that killed Russian military journalist Vladlen Tatarsky in St. Petersburg on Sunday.
Zelensky said while on a tour of the northern Chernihiv region, “About St. Petersburg. I’m not thinking what is going on in St. Petersburg, or in Moscow. They have to think. Russia have to think about their cities. I’m thinking about our country. And our cities.”
Russia has arrested an anti-war activist named Daria Trepova in connection with the explosion that killed Tatarsky and injured at least 32 others at a cafe on Sunday.
Trepova’s husband Dmitry Rylov told the independent Russian publication The Insider that he is convinced his wife “was really just set up and used .”
Some more context: Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said Ukraine may be behind the explosion. “There is evidence that the Ukrainian special services may be involved in the planning of this terrorist attack,” Peskov said. However, no evidence has yet been presented about who carried out the bombing.
Ukraine has said little about the explosion, beyond blaming in-fighting in Russia.
Two independent organizations in Russia — the Libertarian party and Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation — have denied any association with Trepova.
Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich has filed an appeal against his arrest , according to the Russian state news agency TASS.
The agency cited the press service of the Lefortovo court in Moscow, where he was taken into custody last week.
“The court received a complaint from Gershkovich’s defense against the choice of a preventive measure in the form of detention,” TASS reported.
No date for hearing the appeal has been set.
Gershkovich is currently being held in a pre-trial detention center at the notorious Lefortovo prison until May 29. He faces up to 20 years in prison on espionage charges.
It is the first time an American journalist has been detained on accusations by Moscow of spying since the Cold War.
