title: Man who official says has past mental health issues faces hate crime charges after disrupting service at Manhattan synagogue
description: A man who a law enforcement official says has a history of mental health issues has been arrested and charged with multiple hate crimes after disrupting Shabbat services and injuring a woman at Central Synagogue in Manhattan Friday night, New York police said.
author: Mark Morales, Karina Tsui, Rebekah Riess
content:
A man who a law enforcement official says has a history of mental health issues has been arrested and charged with multiple hate crimes after disrupting Shabbat services and injuring a woman at Central Synagogue in Manhattan Friday night, New York police said.
The man, identified as 46-year-old Larry Montes from the Bronx, also “damaged synagogue property,” and spat at and headbutted a member of the synagogue’s security team as he was escorted out of the building, Commissioner Jessica Tisch said on X .
Montes was arraigned Saturday night in criminal court, where a judge set bail at $10,000 cash and $30,000 in bonds, according to the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office. If convicted, Montes could face five to 15 years in prison, the DA said.
Congregants scrambled Friday night as shouts of panic erupted, according to a clip from the synagogue’s livestream obtained by CNN affiliate WCBS . A security guard restrained the man as he barreled down the aisle, according to WCBS.
Montes entered the synagogue during the service and was sitting down for roughly 10 minutes before he got up and was confronted by security, a law enforcement official told CNN.
Security officers began to question him once he started walking toward an area that wasn’t open to the public, prompting him to chop at two candles, each valued around $10,000, with his hands, the official said.
When he tried to make his way toward the rabbi, security escorted him out and he proceeded to attack a woman and the security guard while also yelling a racial slur at him, the official said.
A 63-year-old woman suffered a small cut to her lip and injuries to her right forearm after being struck by the man, an NYPD spokesperson told CNN.
The District Attorney’s office said it has requested full temporary orders of protection for the victims involved.
“He was screaming and yelling. I heard a loud pop … We thought it was a gun,” Susan Roane, who was at the service, told WCBS.
Congregant Arlynn Greenbaum told WCBS she saw the suspect wasn’t armed, but still wanted to take cover.
“He was just ranting and raving and yelling,” she said. “He was very full of hate.”
Montes has several sealed arrests, some of which were robberies, as well as a history of mental health issues, the law enforcement official told CNN. Investigators do not have evidence that he was targeting anyone inside the synagogue, the official said.
While the precise motivation for Friday’s attack remains unclear, it comes amid a rise in reports of antisemitic assaults on American soil. Just last year, the US reached a record high of such attacks , including its first fatality since 2022, according to a report published by the Anti-Defamation League.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has had a tense relationship with some members of the city’s Jewish community over his fierce criticism of Israel’s actions in Gaza, was quick to condemn the attack.
Antisemitic assaults reached a record high in the US last year, Anti-Defamation League report says
“This despicable act has no place in our city, and our administration will do everything in our power to keep Jewish New Yorkers safe,” he said on X on Friday night. He added that New Yorkers must be able to observe their religion without fear of violence.
“I am grateful to Central Synagogue’s security team for swiftly stepping in to prevent more violence, and to the NYPD sergeant who apprehended him and took him into custody,” Mamdani said in a social media post announcing Montes’ charges on Saturday .
“Our administration will always stand against bigotry in all its forms. We will use every tool at our disposal to confront antisemitism and keep Jewish New Yorkers — and all New Yorkers — safe,” the mayor added.
Montes has been charged with “two counts of assault as a hate crime and one count of criminal mischief as a hate crime, along with other charges,” Tisch said.
“I have spoken with the rabbi of the synagogue, and I’m relieved that no one was seriously injured. Those who were hurt were evaluated at the scene and are doing well,” Tisch said.
In a statement posted on Facebook hours after the attack, Central Synagogue said it was grateful for the outpouring of support after Friday’s “disturbing events.”
“We will keep on gathering for joyful, meaningful Judaism with our Central family every week,” the temple wrote.
“We went through something really hard and scary last night,” synagogue cantor Jenna Pearsall said, before offering a “healing prayer … focused on the whole community, on all of us,” during a Shabbat service Saturday morning.
Central Synagogue Rabbi Andrew Kaplan Mandel opened the service on Saturday by saying the congregation is grateful to be safe and won’t “allow anyone to rob us of our attention on Shabbat.”
“Our day of rest was interrupted last night by a security incident in our main sanctuary, but we are OK. We are safe. We are grateful to be here, we are grateful to our security team for supporting us. We feel so grateful for our community,” the rabbi said.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon condemned what he said was an antisemitic attack in a post directly criticizing the city’s leader.
“This is another chilling reminder that anti-Semitism does not belong in the past, it’s occurring here and now, in the heart of New York,” he wrote on X .
New York Governor Kathy Hochul called the attack “appalling.”
“Jewish New Yorkers have every right to worship openly, proudly, and without fear,” she wrote on X.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s David Williams, Emma Tucker and Tina Burnside contributed to this report.

title: Republicans worry their chances of keeping Congress are slipping away. Inside the Trump campaign plan to change that
description: President Donald Trump has finally given the green light to pour millions of dollars from his personal PAC toward boosting vulnerable Republicans in November, two people familiar with the plans told CNN.
author: Alayna Treene, Adam Cancryn, Sarah Ferris
content:
President Donald Trump has finally given the green light to pour millions of dollars from his personal PAC toward boosting vulnerable Republicans in November, two people familiar with the plans told CNN, as some top campaign advisers privately acknowledge that Republicans’ chances of keeping control of both the House and Senate are dwindling.
Trump’s political team is still debating what the final dollar figure will be, though one person familiar with the discussions floated $30 million in the first tranche. Another official cautioned that the final amounts have not yet been decided. The long-awaited cash infusion is happening in the coming weeks, two people said, describing it as the first salvo in a stretch-run effort as November looms just three months away.
And it comes amid growing GOP concerns that severe headwinds over the Iran war and high gas prices could suppress voter turnout.
“There is a path where we keep the House and the Senate,” one source told CNN. “I’m not in a place today where I’m prepared to say we’re cautiously optimistic about that.”
Trump is also belatedly preparing to ratchet up his own campaigning schedule, with plans to travel at least once a week to hold a spate of rallies in battleground districts, one adviser said. His team first promised this move months ago, and Republicans have long argued it’s a crucial step to energizing MAGA voters critical to the party’s midterm chances.
“He loves to travel, but he hates to travel,” said one of his advisers, noting that domestic issues and the Iran war upended early plans to get him on the road more frequently. Trump has recently told his closest aides that he wants to be out more stumping for GOP candidates. But advisers acknowledge his enthusiasm could evaporate just as quickly.
“We’ll see how long that lasts,” the adviser said. “Once he’s traveling, he’s like: ‘Why am I doing this? I want to be doing other things.’”
Still, there’s widespread angst within the party that Trump has waited too long to get more directly involved. Lawmakers and operatives have privately agonized for months over the president’s reluctance to commit his vast sums to helping elect candidates across the country. The GOP is fighting to hold dozens of House districts and a handful of critical Senate seats amid voter backlash over rising prices and the deeply unpopular war in Iran — with no end in sight on either problem.
“President Trump is the unequivocal leader of the Republican party who is committed to maintaining Republicans’ majority in Congress. In just over one year, the President has made our country greater than ever before with the most secure border in American history, the largest middle-class tax cuts ever, and the lowest murder rate since 1900,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement to CNN.
“President Trump will continue to draw a sharp contrast with his commonsense agenda and the radical Democrats in Congress,” she added.
Murder is at lowest rate since the 1950s. Trump touts it as a personal success.
An adviser close to Trump acknowledged that, with the president’s approval ratings scraping new lows, there’s little expectation he can win over large numbers of independents and swing voters — which was part of his path to victory in critical swing states in 2024. Instead, Republicans believe their fate in November rests almost solely on turning out millions of the MAGA faithful who typically don’t vote in midterm elections.
“Without a doubt, we’ve got to make sure we get some of these voters who show up for Donald Trump in presidential elections to show up for these congressionals,” the adviser said.
But in recent months, Trump and Republicans haven’t offered much to energize their base. Congressional Republicans squandered the final weeks before the August recess fighting amongst themselves over legislation — specifically the president’s controversial elections bill that would cement federal voter ID laws and install more voting restrictions, which stands little chance of becoming law and never even made it to the Senate floor.
Congressional GOP leaders have long believed that their success in the midterms will largely hang on Trump’s ability to recreate his 2024 coalition. They need Trump to help turn out as much of his MAGA base as possible in crucial battleground turf — especially in states like Michigan, Ohio and North Carolina, which have critical House and Senate races that could determine control of Congress next January.
Republicans are defending critical blue-state seats too, like the pivotal Senate seat in Maine and several House seats in both New York and California. But the vast majority of this fall’s map is in places where Trump has already proven he can win, like in Iowa and Pennsylvania.
GOP campaign officials have also been urging their candidates from the start to lean in — not away — from Trump on the trail, according to House and Senate campaign operatives. That includes even the most centrist Republicans, like Rep. Mike Lawler, who represents a vulnerable seat in New York’s Hudson Valley and welcomed Trump this spring for a joint rally in one of the reddest parts of his district.
Lawmakers also need him to stay on message, driving out big crowds and turning on his election-year charm with talk of the GOP’s accomplishments on affordability. But Trump has made little headway in selling his domestic accomplishments — or ending a monthslong foreign war that he repeatedly vowed would only last four to six weeks.
In private conversations with Trump, some advisers have sought to emphasize how significantly the war is dragging down Republicans’ chances, arguing that even voters who generally support his goals in Iran are unwilling to stomach a drawn-out conflict that’s raising prices at home.
The prospect of persistently high gas prices has particularly damaged Trump’s standing, people familiar with the internal discussions said, serving as a prominent visual reminder of an affordability crisis that many Americans feel has gotten worse under this administration.
“It’s higher prices; that’s what they’re upset about,” said one of the advisers.
Perhaps reacting to those pressures, both Vice President JD Vance and departing White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt this week started emphasizing that lowering gas prices was equally as or more important to Trump than keeping Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. That’s a shift from Trump’s frequent assertions that Tehran’s nuclear capabilities are all that matters.
“I think both goals are equally as important to the president: We want to keep gas prices low but also ensuring Iran can never get a nuclear weapon. Something he will see through no matter what,” Leavitt told reporters traveling on Air Force One Friday.
Trump has nevertheless insisted publicly that he’s willing to prolong the war for as long as it takes to win it, downplaying the domestic impact even as he struggles to find a clear path toward achieving his aims in the Middle East.
Amid that worsening backdrop, Trump has repeatedly suggested recently that the midterms aren’t really his problem. And in addition to waving off Americans’ economic anxieties and declining to prioritize bringing an end to the Iran war, he’s also emphasized his own pet projects over the broader GOP agenda.
“I don’t have to be supporting all the people. You know, I have a busy schedule,” Trump said in an interview with Punchbowl News last week, adding: “I said to somebody, ‘I won. I’m not campaigning.’”
Those closest to the president insist he still cares deeply about ensuring Republicans win as many races in November as possible. But, one adviser cautioned, he won’t get involved in races he thinks aren’t winnable.
“He doesn’t want to carry dead carcasses across the finish line,” that person said, referencing Trump being incredibly protective of who he chooses to endorse. “He’s not going to endorse a loser and ruin his brand.”
But he does acutely understand that Democrats winning either the House or the Senate in November would have a highly negative impact on his final two years in office, they said.
“The next two years will be f*cking horrible if we lose both chambers. And Trump knows that,” that source said. Other officials have emphasized that Trump does not want to go through the same type of investigations and battles with Congress that he did during his first term, which included two impeachment trials.
The political operation surrounding the president consists of a tight group of loyal advisers who worked on Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and other previous campaigns. It’s run by his former political guru, James Blair, who up until recently served as the White House deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs.
Other high-ranking members of the team include: Chris LaCivita, a co-campagin manager of Trump’s 2024 reelection campaign; Taylor Budowich, who previously ran MAGA Inc. and later led White House communications; Timothy Saler, who previously helmed Trump’s 2024 data operations; and Tony Fabrizio, the president’s longtime pollster.
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who worked alongside LaCivita and the others throughout Trump general election campaign, continues to be heavily involved in all strategy ahead of November, the officials said.
There was a bit of a shakeup this week when Leavitt announced she’s departing her role as press secretary at the end of August, just two months before the midterms. Leavitt has long been viewed inside the West Wing as one of the president’s most effective messengers on the upcoming elections. As of Saturday morning, it was unclear when the role would be replaced.
Those on the team have described their strategy as being guided by the same principles they used to take them across the finish line in 2024. The most crucial aspect, they said, is their data operation. The president’s chief of staff will often remark to the group that everything must be driven by the extensive data they have amassed in recent years and used to energize members of Trump’s base.
“We know exactly who our voters are,” one of the president’s political operatives said. “Based on the data operation, we know how to reach them, and we know what it takes to get them off their ass.”
Trump’s advisers also cite a number of recent political wins they argue should help come November, including Republicans’ unprecedented effort to redraw congressional districts across several states, shifting a handful of seats toward the GOP and further limiting the number of races that are realistically up for grabs. That redistricting push — spurred directly by Trump — is a key reason that Republicans believe they still have a chance to keep the House.
Republicans claimed another victory after the Supreme Court struck down restrictions on the amount that official campaign committees can spend on individual candidates — a change that party operatives insist will help even up the financial arms race given the GOP has far more money than Democrats in PACs and outside groups.
“Our money’s going to go so much further,” one Republican campaign official said following the ruling. “We’re not going out there and saying we’re going to win a gazillion seats … but we feel like we’re probably in the best possible position we’ve been in.”

title: Bulldozers rip into Big Bend National Park, driving anger and heartbreak
description: Environmentalists and a bipartisan coalition of state officials and border sheriffs are part of a growing chorus of opposition to ongoing border security amid the wilds of Big Bend National Park in Texas.
author: Ed Lavandera, Ashley Killough, Rachel Clarke
content:
The towering cliffs, jagged mountain tops, and punishing desert climate of the Big Bend region in Texas have long proved to be the best barrier the United States could have with Mexico. For generations, the idea of needing to build physical structures to stop illegal migration was considered “insane,” as one former superintendent of Big Bend National Park said.
But now the expansive reach of President Donald Trump’s southern border plan has stretched into this remote region that sees only about 1% of unauthorized crossing apprehensions. Bulldozers are clearing land in the beloved national park, where wildlife roams and the scenery has been untouched for thousands of years .
“We didn’t have to worry about any type of barrier. We had a God-made barrier,” said Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland of Terrell County, a vast and sparsely populated area northeast of the park. He spent 26 years in the US Border Patrol, hearing little if any talk of needing extra infrastructure in the area where he grew up, he said. “But that’s definitely changed.”
US Customs and Border Protection says it’s not planning to build the same kind of 30-foot-high barrier that has appeared across parts of Arizona, California, New Mexico and Texas inside the national park. But critics say the plan that is in the works is no less destructive.
Earlier this month, bulldozers were videoed uprooting trees and shoveling dirt as wild animals trotted by. They were doing preliminary work ahead of the budgeted $1.72 billion main construction project designated for the area inside Big Bend National Park, the agency said.
It’s part of the bigger plan to finish the border wall — or some form of it — before Trump leaves office, with steel walls and vehicle barriers and hundreds of miles of new roads cutting through wildly remote areas.
Those with concerns or outright opposition to the work in this remote desert wilderness run the gamut from a few elected Republicans to young activists, sweeping in a pro-border control sheriff and a retired National Park Service superintendent.
Photographer Natalie Newman made a commitment to Big Bend back in February when then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem waived certain federal laws related to environmental safety, historic preservation and wildlife protection, among other initiatives, saying there was “an acute and immediate need to construct additional physical barriers and roads” in the Big Bend region.
“It started out as just documenting the beauty of it, trying to get people to see why it’s special and what makes it special and what makes it so beautiful and worth protecting. But that has transformed just over the last week,” she told CNN, standing near Santa Elena Canyon, where tall cliffs rise nearly 1,500 feet high from the Rio Grande and where she first saw bulldozers working in the national park.
“More than anything else, I feel heartbreak over all of this,” she said. Newman enjoys the wilder parts of this park that’s larger than the state of Rhode Island, where you may see fewer people than javelinas — a mammal that looks like a small wild pig, though it’s an entirely different species. Cacti and wildflowers bloom across the state and federal land around Big Bend, which coupled with even larger nature preserves across the border are part of the Chihuahuan desert, the largest such ecosystem in North America.
But these days when her binoculars are trained on something in the distance, she’s more likely to be checking on the progress of road clearing than on any of the hundreds of bird species that frequent the park. She said she will keep sharing that news, doing her part to stand up for the national park.
“I’m hopeful every single day that it’ll be the day that someone somewhere does something that puts a stop to it,” she said.
If there is no stopping, retired park superintendent Bob Krumenaker said what could happen in Big Bend would rival the flooding of Hetch Hetchy Valley a century ago, an event that changed arguments about preserving the environment. It’s why he labels the whole plan “insane.”
“If they continue with this and build most of the things they have talked about, or even a good fraction of those, this will be the biggest desecration of the national park system — not just Big Bend National Park — since they built a dam in a pristine valley in Yosemite National Park more than 100 years ago. This is a story that our children and grandchildren will be telling,” he told CNN.
Compounding the natural destruction is the damage being done to people’s trust, Krumenaker added.
“It’s just a tremendous erosion, if not violation, of the agreement that Texans and the American people made when they established that national park. The federal government that I worked for for 41 years is disrespecting its citizens in a in a huge way.”
Krumenaker, now chairman of the Keep Big Bend Wild advocacy group, spent five years as superintendent of Big Bend National Park and is familiar not only with the multiple studies and approvals needed for any material changes, but also with his federal partners in Border Patrol and the need for security.
“I totally support a secure border in Big Bend, but this is the least active place in the country for illegal border crossings,” he said. “This is purely political, and it will, it risks destroying one of the nation’s greatest places. It’s just horrible.”
He recalled as superintendent having an annual budget of between $8 million and $9 million and a maintenance to-do list of about $100 million they would chip away at when they could. Those numbers are dwarfed by the $1.72 billion earmarked for the Big Bend work, part of the larger $46.5 billion allocated for border wall construction in Trump’s signature legislation, the “Big Beautiful Bill.”
Sheriff Cleveland thought the talk of security construction was “BS” when he first heard of it.
His experience in local and national law enforcement tells him a different story than that framed by CBP that Big Bend is “an area of high illegal entry.”
What he calls the “God-given barriers” of steep mountains and valleys around the river and an undeveloped landscape without roads would prevent any vehicle getting to his patch. Yet new vehicle barriers are being planned for Terrell County, part of the total $7 billion scheme for the Big Bend sector of the border that includes the national park and land either side.
In a statement to CNN, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said the agency is carrying out “survey and design work,” rather than the construction of a wall through the park. It involves building “one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” he said.
“We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local businesses depend on,” he added.
“I believe in border security … but let’s put a barrier where a barrier makes sense,” Cleveland told CNN. “Let’s spend money where we need to spend the money.”
Cleveland thinks using technology would be better support for him and other rural areas. He points to a solar-powered radar tower with a relatively small footprint that can scan the landscape and identify humans by their gait, triggering cameras to lock on and feed information to agents. Another option would be drones tracking people and helping responders plan a safe interception amid the rugged terrain, he said.
“The biggest problem is the people making the decisions out here for the Big Bend sector have never stepped foot out here.”
Cleveland ran for sheriff as a Republican but says he may switch to independent — what he sees as the profligate federal spending on something unnecessary does not mesh with his own fiscal conservatism.
He signed a letter being carried around the area by former land commissioner Jerry Patterson, praising Trump for closing the border and asking the administration to consider cheaper and less destructive options for the Big Bend region.
A similar approach is being taken by others in Texas.
US Sen. John Cornyn wrote to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin last week urging him to meet with local stakeholders before any more construction proceeds on state or federal property. Some of Mullin’s involvement so far has been to waive another federal law, effectively ending a lawsuit claiming that law was being violated. Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham was more forthright, sending a cease-and-desist letter warning of possible legal action to Customs and Border Protection after she said a federal contractor was sent to work in the Big Bend Ranch State Park without permission. The accompanying news release was titled “Don’t Tread on Texas.”
On Friday, The People of La Junta for Preservation, an Indigenous-led preservation nonprofit, an outdoor recreation company and members of the Lipan Apache community asked a federal court to block the border wall construction on grounds the project threatens constitutionally protected religious freedoms.
The suit, filed in San Antonio, states: “Once an archaeological site excavated by heavy machinery, once the physical context of artifacts is destroyed, or once a sacred or culturally significant landscape is permanently altered, the injury is irreparable.”
The threatened areas, the suit contends, include places members of the Lipan Apache community use “for religious observance, ceremony, prayer, gathering, or other traditional religious practices.”
CNN has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.
The nonprofit said they chose to pursue legal action because their “ancestors entrusted” them with the land. “For us, this is not an abstract policy debate,” the group said in a Facebook post Friday. “Our families have lived, prayed, gathered medicine, buried and reburied our ancestors, carried water, made offerings, and held ceremony along this river for generations beyond written memory. The river is not simply a boundary or a resource. She is living. She is a relative.”
In a separate case filed in the nation’s capital, a federal judge on Friday rejected the Tohono O’odham Nation’s request to block border wall construction along parts of the Native American tribe’s reservation in Arizona. The Nation claimed the wall would trespass on its lands and diminish its boundaries without congressional authorization. US District Judge Richard Leon wrote “the Government’s interests in securing the border, enforcing immigration laws, and ensuring public safety outweigh any surviving irreparable harms at this juncture.” In a statement, Tohono O’odham Nation Chairman Verlon M. Jose disagreed and said the tribe “will consider all possible options for moving forward,” The Associated Press reported.
Gov. Greg Abbott remarked before Trump entered the White House for the first time that he did not want a border wall across the entirety of his state. “There are serpentine regions of the Rio Grande where it would be extremely challenging to build a wall. There are parts like the Big Bend region — we don’t want (to) see a wall in the beautiful Big Bend National Park,” Abbott said in December 2016, as reported by The Associated Press . CNN asked for his current views and was directed to a previous statement from Abbott’s press secretary Andrew Mahaleris: “Rugged, isolated areas like Big Bend are great opportunities to deploy technology to aid in securing the border.”
Critics say most statewide elected Republican officials have been too quiet in their condemnation of the border barrier construction projects because they fear the wrath of Trump’s criticism on his signature issue of border security.
“The one person who is supposed to stand for Texas right now, our governor, is silent,” resident Jess Bartko said. “What they are doing is actively waging a war against our parks, our public lands, our community and our livelihoods.”
On Wednesday, Bartko and about 100 other protesters gathered by the river, whose route gives the area its name and which attracts many of the half-million or so annual visitors to the national park.
Tourism is a big deal here — for running the river and watching the night sky. There are worries that both will be impacted. As far as the upheaval, there could be debris in the river, and construction lights from sites and worker camps could pollute some of the darkest sky in the Lower 48, blurring the star-filled views of the cosmos.
This week some roads and facilities were closed in the national park because of the construction.
Down at the river, beside the entrance to Santa Elena Canyon, one of the “crown jewels” of the park, the demonstrators whooped and hollered, their shouts echoing off the cliff walls as they pledged to keep working to protect Big Bend.
“The land remembers, the water remembers, it will remember us and our fight,” Joan Escamilla told her fellow supporters of the national park. “You can bury my heart in the Rio Grande.”

title: One Cooper Flagg card changed this collector’s life in an instant
description: Jason Williams landed the one-of-a-kind Cooper Flagg NBA debut patch card — and now has multimillion-dollar offers on the table.
author: Andy Scholes
content:
Jason Williams landed the one-of-a-kind Cooper Flagg NBA debut patch card — and now has multimillion-dollar offers on the table.
Williams, a machine shop owner from Clover, South Carolina, suddenly finds himself holding one of the most coveted cards in the sports memorabilia world .
The father of five entered a break of Topps Chrome Update Basketball on Monday and landed the one-of-one Cooper Flagg debut patch card, which has already drawn several multimillion-dollar offers.
Williams told CNN the moment he realized the card was his was surreal.
“When it happened, I mean, I went to the floor like a baby in the fetal position,” Williams said. “I mean, it was just emotional because I knew. I knew what had happened. It took me a few seconds for it to register in my mind, but it was just emotions took over me.”
A “break” is a popular way for collectors to buy sports cards without purchasing an entire box. Typically conducted via livestream, participants purchase the rights to a specific team or player and receive the eligible cards pulled for that team or player from a set number of packs or boxes.
Williams paid $515 for the Dallas Mavericks in a break conducted by Rhody Breakers, based in Rhode Island.
“I was watching it on my phone sitting in the living room,” Williams said. “My 12-year old was getting ready to go to bed. We knew a card that was coming was gonna be a pretty big one. And I knew I had a big team in that break.”
Flagg’s card is one-of-a-kind and features a patch from the jersey he wore in his NBA debut.
As the breaker got closer to revealing the highly sought-after card, Williams decided to move the livestream from his phone to a bigger screen.
“I was like, ‘hey, we need to put this on the big screen’ and my wife was like, ‘OK, whatever, do what you need to do,’” Williams said. “So I put it on.”
Then the card collectors around the hobby had been chasing appeared on the screen.
It belonged to Williams.
“It was intense,” he said.
Williams, who turned 50 in July, said he has collected sports cards on and off since he was 12. He has long enjoyed opening packs himself but discovered online breaks about six years ago.
“It was totally new to me when I’ve seen it, and I’m old school, so the internet stuff I ain’t really into. But this one I figured out, and it was an easy way to do it,” Williams said. “And this one was a $515 break, so it was an expensive one to me, but well worth it.”
Williams said the adrenaline was so intense that he didn’t sleep that night.
“I got in my truck and I drove to the store and got me a Monster Energy drink,” Williams said. “I knew I wasn’t going to sleep that night.”
Instead, Williams stayed up talking with others in the online chat before going to work at 5 a.m.
“I had to just get my mind off of it, but the excitement level and the adrenaline was so intense that, I mean, I don’t even know how to explain that,” he said.
Pittsburgh Pirates offer outrageous trade for one-of-a-kind Paul Skenes baseball card
Now Williams has another decision to make: What does he do with the card?
The Dallas Mavericks have offered lower-level season tickets for 32 years and a package of other perks in exchange for the card. There are also multimillion-dollar offers from others interested in acquiring it.
For now, he says he’s in no rush to make a deal.
“Right now, I’m not even looking at the money,” Williams said.
“For me, I am looking forward to the experiences that I’m gonna get out of this and the things that my family and my kids are going to get to experience that are memories for a lifetime.”

title: The Buffalo Bills’ new stadium has some seats with obstructed views. What’s worse are the ticket prices
description: The Buffalo Bills play their first preseason game at their new Highmark Stadium on Saturday, but season ticketholders got a sneak peek at an open practice last week.
author: Chris Isidore
content:
The Buffalo Bills play their first preseason game at their new Highmark Stadium on Saturday, but season ticketholders got a sneak peek at an open practice last week.
Social media was flooded with photos showing obstructed views of the field from some seats. Even though a handful of fans were upset over sightlines, there is an even bigger problem: how costly attending games will be in the new $2.2 billion stadium.
That includes higher ticket prices and personal seat licenses (PSLs), which just give fans the right to buy season tickets, not the tickets themselves. PSLs cost $750 to $50,000 per seat. That comes on top of the $850 million in taxpayer money already paid to fund construction.
Season ticketholder Angelica James, whose seats between the 20- and 30-yard lines wasn’t blocked, said she chose to go with worse seats this year for the same cost as last season. However, she’s not angry at her team.
“It’s not just the Bills,” she said. “It’s everyone in the world is trying to make money.”
Five other National Football League teams are planning new stadiums in the next five years, in Hammond, Indiana (for the Chicago Bears); Cleveland; Kansas City; Tennessee; and Washington, DC. They are all likely to arrive with their own PSLs, higher ticket prices and more premium seats, meaning fewer cheap ones.
The NFL’s last building boom at the start of this century raised the average cost of tickets by 30% during the first year of a new stadium, according to Victor Matheson, professor of economics at the College of the Holy Cross who specializes in the business of sports. He expects this next round will increase ticket prices by the same percentage, if not more, as well as more expensive PSLs.
PSLs are automatically included in new NFL stadiums, Matheson said, because they are big money makers. Under NFL rules, teams need to share ticket revenue with the rest of the league. But they can keep all of money earned from PSLs. Every NFL team with a new stadium has used them since the Carolina Panthers first introduced them at Ericsson Stadium in 1996.
The Bills raised an estimated $250 million from the sale of PSLs for its new 60,000 - seat stadium, according to Kurt Badenhausen, sports business reporter for Sportico. That comes out to an average of about $4,000 per seat.
That’s what fans pay on top of the season ticket prices, which in the case of Highmark, can be double to comparable seats in the old stadium.
James and her husband, Cameron, were prepared to pay for PSLs along with somewhat higher ticket prices. But when they attended a meeting for season ticketholders, they discovered the seats they had purchased for $4,300 each last year would now cost $8,610.
“In our minds, even if it was $10,000 each for the PSL, and the tickets had gone up a little bit, that we would have been okay with that. But we walked out of that meeting being completely shocked,” she told CNN.
She and her husband decided to not re-up their club seats that came with various amenities, including coverage from weather and a private bar and bathroom. Instead, they downgraded to general admission seats at the same cost with PSLs of “only” $6,000 each.
For fans who don’t downgrade, however, new stadiums do have more bells and whistles, like wider seats and better concourses and concessions. Part of the reason new stadiums have higher ticket prices is because the fans are hypothetically getting a lot more for their money, according to Marc Ganis, a sports business consultant who works with the NFL and numerous teams.
“At least theoretically, everything related to the fan experience will be better,” he said.
However, new amenities require more room. That leads to fewer overall seats, and the cheap ones are being eliminated. For example, the Bills’ old stadium had a capacity to seat 71,600 versus 60,000 in the new one.
But it’s mainly strong demand for tickets, along with fewer seats, driving prices higher. The Bills website shows no season tickets are left for sale.
“Demand for live audience experiences came back with a vengeance after Covid, and it and it seems to have persisted,” Matheson said. “The number of tickets being sold in the NFL has stayed pretty constant over the last two decades because we haven’t added new franchises and stadiums aren’t getting any bigger.”
Following the complaints about obstructed views, Bills team executives told the media that many of those seats are being sold for events like concerts, not games. Less than 1% of fans, they added, had complained.
But for any fan with a railing or a cable in their sightlines, they are going to be unhappy after shelling out additional dollars.
“It might be a small percentage of people, but its still a lot of people,” said Sportico’s Badenhausen. “For those 600 or so fans, it’s a 100% of their seats being obstructed.”

title: Jalen Brunson on the ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball
description: There is an ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball. CNN Sports talked with New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson about the connection.
author: Omar Jimenez
content:
There is an ever-growing love story between the game of golf and basketball .
Maybe it’s the rhythm of a smooth swing mirroring the comfort of a polished jumper. Maybe it’s the chance to perform outside in front of chirping birds rather than chirping fans inside a booming arena.
For NBA champion and Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, it’s simpler than that – it’s competition.
“My dad stopped playing me one-on-one on the court, so I needed to find something else to beat him in,” Brunson told CNN Sports . “You’re still being competitive.”
Brunson’s dad, Rick Brunson, was also an NBA player and is currently an assistant coach for the New York Knicks .
“There are a lot of players around the league who bring clubs on the road when you’re going to warm cities,” the younger Brunson said. “It’s become a thing.”
The offseason especially has turned into showcase opportunities for players across social media and beyond, either casually or in tournament form.
Brunson’s annual charity golf classic fits right in. It raises money for his Second Round Foundation, which pulls on his story as a second-round draft pick to provide opportunities to “the overlooked” and stresses “success doesn’t always look like a first-round pick,” the foundation’s mission statement reads.
“You can go down so many different roads with that term,” Brunson told CNN. “I felt like I was overlooked in sport, but there are a lot of kids and people who overlooked this in life.”
He co-founded the foundation with his mom, Sandra Brunson.
“Overlooked is a term that I think many people can associate with,” but for children “everyone needs to start on the same playing field and we’re just happy to be able to help and to provide whatever resources we can,” Sandra Brunson told CNN Sports.
For the golf fundraiser, Brunson said he typically sends invites out to other players, like teammate Josh Hart, but that people also sign up on their own before his mom cut him off.
“I send the invites, OK? So if anybody didn’t get one, it’s on me,” Sandra said.
Jalen laughed and said, “I mean, I was gonna throw her under the bus anyway.”
LeBron James , whom Brunson is scheduled to be facing on opening day of the coming NBA season, is among the basketball elite attempting to climb the golfing ladder.
Others, more notoriously prolific on the course, like Steph Curry, Los Angeles Lakers star Austin Reaves, Michael Jordan, and even recently retired guard JR Smith have arguably climbed that ladder.
Curry won the 2023 American Century Classic, a premier celebrity tournament that includes many pro athletes. Reaves has a fully dedicated golf social media Instagram account , and right after retirement from the NBA, Smith joined the golf team at North Carolina A&T as a freshman walk-on.
Even Caitlin Clark and Diana Taurasi on the WNBA side have not been shy about their golf bug.
The NBA posted a video of Philadelphia 76ers star Tyrese Maxey on the course as he jokingly admitted, “I can do all this basketball with 20,000 people but golfing in front of cameras? Can’t do it.”
The PGA published an article citing specific basketball movements that “closely relate to the golf swing and golf performance,” including: free throws compared with putting, the crossover compared with the tempo change during a swing, and more.
For Brunson, though, it’s not that deep – yet.
“It can be,” he said. “But I’m getting there.”
“There’s a lot surrounding it that makes it like the perfect getaway for a lot of not just basketball players but pro athletes,” Brunson said, correctly mentioning the golf phenomenon is nowhere near limited solely to basketball.
But on how prevalent it is in the NBA, he says, “It’s definitely a good group … It’s a perfect getaway where you’re still being competitive.”
One person in the Brunson orbit who hasn’t quite been able to break into the game of golf is Jalen’s mom.
“No one in my family has ever even attempted to invite me to a golf outing to participate,” Sandra told CNN Sports.
“I haven’t seen her even touch a club,” Jalen joked. “And we’re trying to play, we’re not – this isn’t a lesson.”
“My daughter has clubs. My granddaughter has clubs, I don’t even have clubs,” Sandra said.
But it’s also the focal point of their annual charity event so she anticipates her competitiveness as a former collegiate athlete will get her there at some point.
This offseason for Jalen has meant less golf as he recovers from a wrist surgery, but it’s also meant more downtime, valuable moments with family, and even an upcoming children’s book .
Still, the first offseason as an NBA champion has been a little “hectic,” he explained, but in the end “all great problems to have.”
In about two short months, the NBA regular season will officially kick off, but if the volume of offseason golf is any indication, the competitiveness started well before that opening tip.

title: Teen charged with murder of mother and brother used ChatGPT to create ‘fantasy stories’ about killing family, officials say
description: A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said.
author: Karina Tsui, Rebekah Riess
content:
A Massachusetts teen charged in the double murder of his mother and younger brother had used the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT to search for “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories” about the killing of his family, prosecutors have said.
A plea of not guilty was entered Thursday for Arjun Aravind, 17, on two counts of murder, two counts of assault and battery on a family or household member and other charges. His mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14, were found dead Tuesday in their home in Acton, some 20 miles northwest of Boston, prosecutors said .
Arjun Aravind “had recently been demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family,” Middlesex County District Attorney Marian Ryan told reporters Wednesday, citing the law enforcement investigation.
“He was engaged in the use of ChatGPT in creating fantasy stories, kind of the Gothic novel kind of stories, asking questions, creating characters, asking what about this, if this happened to that, and they seem to appear to relate to threats to his family not surviving,” Ryan said .
A “heavily damaged bloody laptop,” and “a bent utensil, possible [sic] a knife with an orange handle” were found at the scene, a police report obtained by CNN affiliate WCVB indicated. Venkatesan’s and Siddharth’s causes of death are still pending, Ryan said.
Aravind over the past year had had behavior issues and his family had hidden knives from him, the teen’s father said, WCVB reported, citing police reports.
The teen did not realize his mother and brother were dead until after he was arrested, his defense attorney, Debra DeWitt, told WCVB. CNN has asked her for comment.
AI technology allegedly has been linked to other criminal acts, and Florida this spring sued ChatGPT owner OpenAI , alleging the tool had “no parental oversight,” got minors addicted, caused users to lose “critical thinking skills,” helped mass shooters and encouraged suicide.
OpenAI believes minors “need significant protection” and has “put in place industry leading protections and policies,” it has said. CNN reached out Friday to OpenAI about this week’s murder case.
Aravind was ordered held without bail and to undergo a mental health evaluation. A probable cause hearing was set for September 11.
Florida sues OpenAI, alleging it’s unsafe for children
Police responded Tuesday to his family home after a tutor arrived for a scheduled visit and could not get in, Ryan said Wednesday in a news conference. The teen’s father was then notified and requested a wellness check.
Officers found the two victims inside – but not Aravind, who was believed to have fled using his mother’s 2014 green Honda Accord, she said. While responding to a separate incident Wednesday morning, police in neighboring Wayland found Aravind in his mother’s car in a parking lot and took him into custody.
The family had only recently moved to Acton for “better schools and support system for the kids,” DeWitt said.
“We put an enormous weight on our kids … We know the kids will be seeing and reading about this, likely on social media,” Ryan said. “This is an unspeakable tragedy. It is an incredibly dark day – obviously, an insurmountable tragedy for the dad in this case.”

title: The obsession with ‘Mamdani marts’ isn’t about groceries
description: Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open five government-owned supermarkets in New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media.
author: Nathaniel Meyersohn
content:
Whenever Mayor Zohran Mamdani offers new details about his plan to open five government-owned supermarkets in New York City, photos of Boris Yeltsin start circulating on social media.
Taken during Yeltsin’s trip to America months before the fall of the Soviet Union in 1989, the photos show the former Russian president astonished by the variety of frozen foods at Randall’s supermarket in Houston. Yeltsin tasted free cheese samples and surveyed the fish. He left the store with a goodie bag.
On the flight after the impromptu stop, Yeltsin sat motionless with his head in his hands, considering the bare shelves of Soviet food markets. “What have they done to our poor people?” he said , according to his biography.
Then, as now, America’s supermarkets are a marvel of the free market. The idea that government, which has been defined as incompetent and inefficient for decades, could provide grocery abundance and variety better than Walmart and Costco has triggered a visceral reaction among critics. They imagine “Mamdani marts” ending up like dreary state-run Soviet stores with one type of soup.
The response to Mamdani’s plan reflects something much deeper than the brand of ketchup public stores will sell or the price of eggs. It comes down to a fundamental disagreement about the responsibility of government.
Where supporters see government intervening to solve problems of everyday people struggling to afford groceries, others see a socialist mayor overreaching to take aim at a powerful symbol of America’s riches.
“The debate is not really about the specific mechanics of the model,” said Nevin Cohen, an associate professor at the CUNY School of Public Health. It’s a “test of competing ideas about what we expect government to provide.”
Never mind that the public stores aren’t a radical new idea and the city is bringing in private operators to manage them and source the food. Or that 99% of New Yorkers will never shop at one of them. They will not destroy John Castimatidis’ Gristedes supermarket empire .
The American supermarket, with its endless array of products and innovations like the shopping cart and barcodes, has achieved an almost mythical status around the world. Supermarkets helped America project democracy abroad and win the Cold War. For decades, the U.S. Information Agency distributed images of supermarkets to promote the benefits of the “American way of life.”
They are a bounty of consumer choice. Between 1960 and 2010, the number of different products in an average US supermarket grew from 6,000 to 47,000. New business models such as Walmart supercenters, Costco warehouse clubs and Trader Joe’s specialty stores expanded the abundance further.
“Food is a potent symbol and catalyst for people’s politics,” said Tracey Deutsch, a historian at the University of Minnesota who studies food and capitalism. Stores were contested sites during the civil rights movement and the pandemic , she noted.
“There’s a sense that grocery stores are the last bastion,” she said. “Grocery stores are places where people make their stand for the world they want.”
Supporters of private sector solutions to address food insecurity say New York City should make it easier for Walmart to open or pay for Costco memberships for people who can’t afford them.
But Mamdani’s animating political philosophy is to use government to solve everyday problems in people’s lives.
He is following in the footsteps of his political idol, Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia, a champion of government intervention during the New Deal who built public parks, housing and the airport that bears his name. Overcoming opposition from private industry, LaGuardia opened a network of city-run indoor markets during the 1930s to move pushcart vendors off streets and reduce the cost of groceries. Several of the markets are open today.
Mamdani wants to turn the vacant sites, still owned by the city, into public grocery stores.
LaGuardia “believed in a simple definition of the task of government to make people’s lives better,” Mamdani said last month. “We are one step closer to fulfilling that fundamental responsibility.”

France has the haute cuisine, the Michelin pedigree and the UNESCO-recognized bread.
Mexico has the confluence of Indigenous and European influences, the slow-cooked meat, and the pre-Hispanic corn processes.

Bethlehem’s rich legacy as a historic 18th-century Moravian settlement has also earned recognition as one of the United States’ newest UNESCO World Heritage sites.

title: New premium airplane seats have a big problem — and it could be getting worse
description: Airlines are building business-class suites so complex and customized that safety regulators can’t approve them in time — potentially leaving brand-new cabins flying empty.
author: Edward Russell
content:
Imagine booking a ticket on one of Europe’s premier airlines, stepping onto a brand-new, ultra-modern Airbus A350, and walking past 34 of the grandest business-class suites in the sky — only to be told no one is allowed to sit in them.
That ironic reality may await passengers on KLM’s new Amsterdam-Toronto route this fall, among other major carriers. The luxury pods — complete with lie-flat beds and sliding privacy doors — could be entirely off-limits when departure day rolls around, sitting completely empty at 35,000 feet.
The culprit isn’t a lack of demand, but a paradox of modern aviation. As premium seats have become increasingly complex, getting regulatory clearance to fly them is harder than ever, creating a production bottleneck that is about to become visible in the sky.
And it’s not just affecting KLM. Airlines around the world are currently plagued by delays in their efforts to deliver new premium offerings — including increasing passenger demand for privacy, high-tech connectivity and inflight entertainment — to meet the surge in air travel . Flagship carriers including American, Lufthansa, Riyadh Air and Singapore Airlines are all struggling to navigate the lengthy, multi-year approval process for bespoke cabins.
How did we get to a place where seats are actually too fancy to fly in? It starts by rewinding the tape a few decades.
When the McCallister family dashes onto their flight to Paris in the 1990 film “Home Alone,” barely making it after an alarm clock failure, the parents — having waved their kids into coach — turn left into first class and settle into what were essentially comfortable, oversized recliners.
That was the standard for decades until British Airways introduced the world’s first lie-flat seat in 2000. In the decades since, front-row real estate has transformed into high-tech mini-apartments.
Take Lufthansa’s new premium Allegris suites and Senses, its sister carrier Swiss’ version. Both are a complete overhaul of their long-haul cabins, featuring seat heating, seat cooling and personal climate controls. Yet, as nice as those amenities are, every added feature introduces a fresh regulatory hurdle, in this case contributing to a multi-year delay before both airlines were able to deploy.
Experts estimate that certifying a new premium seat today takes at least six months longer than it did prior to the Covid pandemic, when lead times averaged one to two years.
Why reclining seats are vanishing from airplanes
“By the time you imagine it, design it, test it, get it certified, get it built — it is a lengthy three-year process,” Ben Minicucci, the CEO of Alaska Airlines, said in May on bringing the airline’s first-ever business-class suites to market. “We approved this design on a new product last year and now it’s getting the seat manufacturers aligned.”
Compounding the crisis is the fact that airlines are actively resisting standardization in a bid to outdo each other.
“Another industry that is in a booming ramp-up phase, you want to scale it — you would go for standardization,” said Mark Hiller, the CEO of seat manufacturer Recaro. Instead, airlines are insisting on custom designs to stand out. “The interest and need for differentiation … are driving the demand and really lead to bottlenecks in the industry.”
Federal regulators are also taking a much harder line on crash safety tests for custom setups. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told The Wall Street Journal in May that the agency sees premium seats “that just don’t pass our human factors tests for impact.”
The obsession with privacy is a massive part of the problem.
“If you went back 10 years ago, there were very few walls in the business-class cabin and today there are a lot,” Andrew Nocella, chief commercial officer of United Airlines, commented earlier this year. “I do think that the evolution of the cabins has made [certification] very complicated.”
United seems to have found a way through the regulatory maze, launching its updated Polaris suites complete with privacy doors on Boeing 787s less than a year after unveiling them in 2025. Nocella says the company worked closely with safety inspectors and manufacturers.
But for most carriers, every added wall, higher door and high-tech widget is another tangle of testing and paperwork.
Modern suites aren’t just big chairs anymore. They are elaborate pieces of architecture packed with complex and heavy new inflight entertainment screens and seat textiles, which populate cabins more densely than ever before . As ZIM Aircraft Seating Group CEO Raffael Rogg points out, every custom material and hard barrier has implications for dynamic impact testing, flammability and crucial Head Injury Criteria safety ratings.
Airline forced to rebalance planes because first class seats are too heavy
Every link in the aviation chain — airlines, planemakers, seat suppliers and regulators — is eager to clear the logjam. No manufacturer wants a multimillion-dollar jet sitting on the tarmac awaiting chairs or flying across the Atlantic carrying ghost suites.
“How do you identify risk with the customers early on and push that risk upstream?” Stephanie Pope, the CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, recently commented about seat certification delays. “There’s nothing our engineers can’t solve, it’s more the time that it takes to solve, and if you’re finding it towards the end of the process that’s going to cause some delivery challenges.”
Part of the solution is fixing predictable design flaws — like ensuring flight attendants can actually see passengers over high privacy walls — early in the development process to avoid last-minute delays. The FAA says it is actively collaborating with international safety partners to streamline approvals, but seat executives warn that throwing extra staff at the problem may not be enough to catch up with market demand.
“In the certification , authorities [and] the seat suppliers are ramping up,” said Recaro CEO Mark Hiller. “On the other hand, all these improvements are somehow eaten up by the more demand we’re having.” In fact, Hiller warns, the bottleneck could get worse before it gets better.
The best passenger airplanes of all time — ranked by CNN’s top aviation expert
KLM is a case in point. In an effort to avoid custom-design traps, the Dutch carrier chose an off-the-shelf model from seat manufacturer Stelia that was already flying on sister airline Air France. Yet despite taking the safer route, KLM’s new A350 business suites remain blocked off, awaiting the green light from European regulators EASA, which KLM says is now using a “revised interpretation of regulatory requirements.”
Delays or not, the airline industry has no plans to turn its back on luxury.
“The complex interiors I don’t see going away,” Boeing’s Pope said. “I think that is the wave of the future.”
She joked: “Someday we’ll all have a shower next to our seat.”
Until then, passengers will just have to hope the seat itself gets certified first.

title: The life-altering choices immigrant families are making under Trump’s crackdown
description: A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for – or avoid – an encounter with immigration authorities.
author: Maria Santana
content:
A quiet upheaval is unfolding in homes, schools, churches and workplaces across the United States, as families try to prepare for –– or avoid –– an encounter with immigration authorities.
Some have left the United States after decades of building lives here. Others have considered giving up their unborn child for adoption, so the baby could have a better future.
Parents are naming guardians for their children in case they are detained or deported, while others have stopped working, shopping or even leaving home, relying instead on neighbors and churches.
The choices are deeply personal. Some are irreversible.
Emma Confesor was pregnant with her fourth child when a question she had never imagined began keeping her awake: Would her baby have a better future raised by someone else?
Confesor, 39, emigrated from Puebla, Mexico, more than two decades ago. But uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s effort to end birthright citizenship led her to consider placing her unborn child up for adoption.
“It didn’t seem fair to me that the baby wouldn’t have citizenship,” Confesor said through tears. “I had considered adoption so the baby could have a better future.”
For weeks, the possibility consumed her. She said she struggled to sleep, afraid her child could be denied the future she believed every baby born in the United States should have.
Confesor was not alone.
Civil rights groups ask judge to block Trump’s new birthright citizenship order
In an ACLU lawsuit challenging Trump’s executive order, another pregnant woman said she became so desperate to ensure her son would be born a US citizen that she asked her doctor whether labor could be induced early so he would arrive before the policy could take effect. Her doctor advised against it.
Then came the decision that changed everything.
On June 30, the Supreme Court ruled that the 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship, rejecting the administration’s effort to end automatic citizenship for children born on U.S. soil to many noncitizen parents.
For Confesor, the fear that had dominated her pregnancy began to lift.
“I feel relieved,” she said. “I kept thinking, ‘It’s not fair.’ I wasn’t sleeping well because I was worried this could affect me. Not just me, but so many mothers who are going to have babies here.”
While Confesor feared for her baby’s future, other parents were preparing for the possibility that they would not be there to raise their children who were born US citizens.
In Maryland, a Salvadoran mother signed legal papers naming Father Vidal Rivas, the priest at her local church, as temporary guardian of her 7-year-old son if she and her husband were deported.
“It’s not easy to sign a document where it feels like you’re handing your child over to someone else,” she told CNN affiliate Univision through tears.
The uncertainty, she said, had taken a toll.
“I keep thinking and thinking… I feel like my health has suffered because you just don’t know,” she said. “Honestly, I’ve stayed in my house, just praying that God’s will be done.”
She is part of a growing number of immigrant parents making contingency plans in case they are detained or deported.
Many families have already been forced into separation. A CNN investigation published last September found more than 100 US citizen children , from newborns to teenagers, had been left without their parents after immigration enforcement actions. Some were taken in by relatives, neighbors or family friends. Others entered foster care.
At St. Matthew’s Episcopal Church in Hyattsville, Maryland, Rivas has been appointed standby legal guardian for at least 31 children whose parents fear they could be detained or deported
“Many of these parents have no other relatives in the country,” Rivas said. “Some want their children to stay here. I would become legally responsible for them so they can continue going to school and have what they need. Other parents hope their children can finish high school before they are sent to reunite with them.”
Rivas said he will serve as a guardian for as long as families need him. “It’s truly as if they were your own children,” he said.
For others, departure has become the only choice that still feels like their own.
Abdiel and Adilene Domínguez had built nearly their entire lives in Minnesota. Abdiel arrived from Mexico at six, Adilene as an infant, and both were protected under Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals , or DACA, which grants certain immigrants brought to the US as children temporary protection from deportation and authorization to work, but no permanent legal status.
They married, raised four children, bought a home and opened a church in Minneapolis.
New Trump rule makes it harder for some immigrants to get green cards
But as immigration enforcement increased, they told CNN they became afraid to go to stores or send their children to school. Abdiel also said he was told his commercial driver’s license would be canceled.
Instead of waiting to see what might happen, they sold their home, vehicles and belongings and left for Mexico.
Seven months later, they were living with Abdiel’s mother in Morelos, where the children were struggling with Spanish and enrolling in school, and their parents were trying to adjust to a country that no longer felt familiar.
“I don’t know anything about Mexico,” Adilene told CNN. “Everything I know is Minnesota. I’m in shock.”
The Dominguezes left on their own, without using a federal program. But the pressure they described mirrors a broader Trump administration strategy encouraging immigrants to depart voluntarily .
Project Homecoming, a $915 million initiative, offers free flights and stipends of up to $2,600 to immigrants who leave through the CBP Home app. An internal DHS document reviewed by CNN in March showed nearly 72,000 people had departed through the program; more than half were already in ICE detention when they enrolled.
More than 72,000 immigration court cases also ended in voluntary departure so far in this fiscal year, compared with more than 35,000 the previous year.
The consequences are also reshaping the lives of US citizens in mixed-status families.
In Pittsburgh, CNN followed Julio Mendoza, an undocumented Mexican immigrant who had lived in the United States since he was 11, as he prepared to leave with his American wife, Sasha, and their three US-born children.
Sasha said they feared Julio could be detained one day and simply not come home. Rather than risk that outcome, the entire family chose to move to Mexico together.
“Everything we do, we do together,” Julio told CNN.
For families who stay, the disruption often unfolds quietly, in the routines they begin to abandon.
Across the country, immigrants have stayed home from work, kept children out of school and avoided stores, churches and other places that once anchored daily life.
Jacobita Cortes, a United Methodist pastor in Chicago, said that fear has changed the rhythms of her community. “They’re afraid to go to the store, to the supermarket,” Cortes told CNN. “Where do our people go? To the supermarkets where you buy your tortillas, your meat; to the church where you go to thank God.”
Some churches, she said, have moved services online, while congregations are helping families who are too afraid to leave home order groceries or arrange school pickups through neighbors and volunteers.
“If someone needs somebody to go do their shopping, they only have to pick up the phone and call,” Cortes said. For parents who are afraid, she added, “find someone who can help, a neighbor or someone who can pick up the children from school.”
The same pattern has surfaced elsewhere. In Minneapolis and New Orleans, CNN found once-bustling shops and restaurants growing quiet during federal immigration operations as some immigrants avoided work and parents kept children home from school.
In Brooklyn’s Little Haiti, normally busy streets and businesses have grown quiet after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haitians .
Community leaders also warned of ripple effects in hospitals, nursing homes and home health care, where many Haitian immigrants work.
For some immigrants, the fear is no longer confined to the possibility of deportation. It is reshaping what it means to live a life in the United States.
CNN’s Carolina Peguero, Priscilla Alvarez, Zoe Sottile, Blake Ellis , Melanie Hicken, Anna-Maja Rappard and Kyung Lah contributed to this report

title: Former Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism found dead
description: Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge professor, was found dead in London on Friday, just days after resigning over questions surrounding his career.
author: Ivana Kottasová
content:
Jason Arday, a former University of Cambridge professor, was found dead in London on Friday, just days after resigning over questions surrounding his career.
A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police told CNN that a 41-year-old man was found unresponsive in Battersea, south London, and was later pronounced dead at the scene. The spokesperson said the death was “treated as as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.”
While the force did not name Arday, British media widely reported that he was the man found dead in Battersea.
Arday, a sociologist, was celebrated as the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge until last month, when allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments began to swirl in the media.
The university’s Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice said in a statement on Friday that the university was “desperately saddened to hear this tragic news.”
“Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” she added in the statement posted on X.
When Arday resigned in early August, he defended himself, saying his decision to step down “should not be interpreted as a loss of faith in scholarship.”
“Nor should it be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me,” he said. “It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.”
News of his death on Friday caused shock waves online, with many criticizing some of the coverage that led to and followed his resignation.
“Quite a bit of the British media should ask themselves some serious questions as to whether the tenor and volume of the coverage they gave to this man was remotely proportionate,” journalist Lewis Goodall said on X.
The Good Law Project, a campaign group that has supported Arday since the allegations first emerged, said Arday’s death was “a tragedy for him and those who loved him.”
The group’s executive director Jo Maugham said in a statement that people around Arday “had been warning the media that this was a risk.”
“I do not understand what the public interest was in continuing to hound him after he resigned as a professor and I do not understand what risk assessments media outlets did,” he added.
Lucy Powell, the UK’s secretary of state for education, said she was “shocked and saddened” to hear about Arday’s death. “My heartfelt condolences are with his friends and family at this very sad time. I urge people to give them privacy through this incredibly difficult period (and) to remember there are real people with loved ones involved.”
Cambridge initially stood by Arday when questions about his qualifications were raised publicly by the British press and a one-time philosophy researcher who left the university after his critique of diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
The university said at the time that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday’s doctorate.
It later opened an investigation, “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appointments,” it said in a statement.
Earlier this week, the university said that Durham and Glasgow Universities were also investigating the circumstances surrounding Arday’s academic posts there.
